extracted.intended_audience: historians of science, scientific authors, and readers interested in Darwin's methods and scientific practice
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging or producing scientific monographs and geological/natural-history writings, covering intellectual scope, workmanship, presentation, and necessary disciplinary training. Emphasises what makes such work durable, useful to specialists and beginners, and scientifically sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great breadth of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Work should show a broad, encompassing perspective that comes from practical study and deep reflection; the author must have 'practically studied and profoundly reflected on the questions discussed'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geikie's remark: 'Great breadth of view. No one who had not practically studied and profoundly reflected on the questions discussed could have written it.' Implies coverage across related subfields and the ability to place specific results in wider context; anti-pattern: narrow, parochial treatment that ignores related lines of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific insight and identification of lines of enquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The author should display uncommon insight by pointing out productive lines of enquiry that will elucidate geological (or domain) problems, often anticipating future fruitful research directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geikie: 'The insight so remarkable... The way in which he points out lines of enquiry that would elucidate geological problems is eminently typical of him.' Guidance: highlight open questions and concrete avenues for follow-up work; scoring note: originality and future usefulness of suggested enquiries raise quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest and sympathetic treatment for readers
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment should put readers into harmony with the author: be inviting, show how delightful the field is, and motivate engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geikie: 'Interesting and sympathetic treatment. The author at once puts his readers into harmony with him. He gives them enough of information to show how delightful the field is to which he invites them.' Guidance: balance enthusiasm with clarity; anti-pattern: dry, alienating exposition that fails to engage non-specialist readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of broad sketch with instructive detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a broad sketch accessible to general readers while including enough detail to instruct and guide beginners and start them on the right track.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geikie: 'There is a broad sketch of the subject which everybody can follow, and there is enough of detail to instruct and guide a beginner and start him on the right track.' Practical guidance: include overviews plus concrete examples, methods, or tasks for novices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability: focus on principles that stand the test of time
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasise underlying principles and lines of thought that are likely to remain valid, even if specific factual details must later be revised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geikie: 'With what unerring instinct he seems to have fastened on the principles that would stand the test of time.' Scoring: favour authors whose conceptual framework remains useful across later developments; allow for corrections in particulars without penalising core insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical training and detailed empirical work
rubrics_metrics.description: Major scholarly value comes from extensive, patient, hands-on empirical work that trains judgment and provides a secure factual base (e.g., monographing a taxon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Huxley: praised the 'years of patient toil' and the Cirripede monograph as necessary training. Guidance: reward thorough, primary-data-based study; anti-pattern: speculative synthesis without grounded empirical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical self-discipline acquired by detailed scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Doing detailed, labour-intensive work cultivates critical habits that prevent careless or overreaching speculative claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Huxley: monographing 'was a piece of critical self-discipline' that 'saved him from endless errors of detail.' Authors should show evidence of having done meticulous groundwork; scoring: evidence of checking, synonyms, indices, and careful descriptions scores highly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of over-speculation beyond observational basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat accepted statements of fact as exhaustive bases for broad speculative deductions; be cautious about deductions that outstrip the limits of observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Huxley: warns against treating accepted facts 'as if they were not only correct, but exhaustive' and then deducing boldly. Guidance: clearly demarcate observation vs speculation, give uncertainty, and limit grand claims unsupported by data; anti-pattern: deductive leaps from incomplete empirical foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire relevant disciplinary breadth (anatomy, development, taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors tackling classificatory or evolutionary questions should acquire working knowledge of related disciplines (e.g., anatomy, embryology, physiology) to strengthen arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Huxley: Darwin 'needed... acquaintance with Anatomy and Development' and would have benefited from 'a special study of embryology and physiology.' Practical guidance: collaborate or train in neighboring fields; mention limitations if such expertise is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness in presentation: plates, figures, indices, and exhaustive descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Monographs should include comprehensive illustrations, multiple figures per plate where needed, and full indexing to reflect the labour and to make the work a reliable reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes the two volumes with 'forty plates, some of them with thirty figures, and the fourteen pages of index' as evidence of labour. Guidance: include visual documentation and robust indexing; scoring: completeness of figures and accessibility of reference apparatus matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent editorial choices to enhance readability and audience fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Edit editions to suit the intended readership: cut overlong discussions, add or reduce technical material, adjust formatting (e.g., printing species/genera in romans) and spacing for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin's notes on second edition: 'cut down into half the mercilessly long discussion', 'I have printed all names of species and genera in Romans', and suggestions like opening interspaces for readability. Guidance: tailor level and presentation to audience; anti-pattern: failure to adapt style/format for accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non-technical material where appropriate for broader appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Including non-scientific or descriptive passages can broaden appeal and provide context; authors should consider balancing technical and general-interest content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin remarks on missing 'non-scientific [parts]' and values a less scientific air for wider readership. Guidance: consider adding anecdotes, natural-history vignettes, or contextual commentary to engage non-specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of honest labour and earnestness in producing scientific works
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of writing is evidence of earnest effort and labour; honest, careful work—however unglamorous—matters intrinsically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin: 'the only object in writing a book is a proof of earnestness, and that you do not form your opinions without undergoing labour of some kind.' Guidance: reward sustained effort and transparent methodology; anti-pattern: superficial or performative scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity in presentation of arguments and avoidance of heterogeneous or confusing organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure should help readers follow the author's course; avoid heterogeneous or poorly-signposted chapters that confuse the reader's geographic or conceptual path.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin's critique of Lyell: missed general headings, early paragraphs tracing a course through many places were 'disturbing'; he 'cut your map loose' to follow more easily. Guidance: use clear headings, maps, and signposting; consider removing distracting dense place-lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair critical appreciation of honest, good work in all classes of scientific labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise and not depreciate the labours of less glamorous scientific workers (cataloguers, hod-men of science) provided their work is honest and good of its kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's attitude: 'he would never allow a depreciatory remark to pass unchallenged on the poorest class of scientific workers, provided that their work was honest, and good of its kind.' Guidance: peer reviewers and authors should evaluate on quality and honesty, not prestige of task.
